performers: National Symphony Orchestra of London, Stanford Robinson
question: How does Robinson pace the waltz after the introductory cadenza?
intro: Stanford Robinson’s National Symphony Orchestra of London recorded this side at Kingsway Hall on 18 January 1945. Decca released it in September; the player preserves the first side without joining the continuation.

cues.title: Recording and release differ
cues.text: The source gives 18 January 1945 for the Kingsway Hall session and September 1945 for the first release. These are different events: neither is the date this digital file was uploaded.
cues.evidence: Commons identifies the session, first release, Decca K1144 and matrix AR9079-2.

cues.title: After the cadenza
cues.text: The early waltz emerges from a quieter region after the introduction. Compare its melodic span with Stokowski’s at the mapped musical position, not at the same elapsed second.
cues.evidence: The 1:12 boundary follows the low 1:10 window; the shared alignment begins at 72 seconds in this file. Existing score-informed notes establish the principal-waltz function.

cues.title: The answering phrase gains weight
cues.text: A fuller span follows the relatively light start of the waltz. Listen for the long melodic shape continuing across the regular accompaniment.
cues.evidence: The strong 1:48 boundary follows a rise from −18.1 dB at 1:35 to −10.0 at 1:45; the following windows remain stronger.

cues.title: Later music on the side
cues.text: The source side continues beyond the common window and reaches stronger late passages. It ends before the complete waltz does; do not read the shorter file as evidence of a faster whole performance.
cues.evidence: The highest windows fall at 2:45–3:10. The comparison ends at 158 seconds here; the source is the first side of a two-sided recording.

composer.epithet: He used the timing of dance and theatre to make a symphony’s return, interruption or collapse physically audible.
facts: Imperial School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck supplied an allowance from 1877 to 1890; their correspondence became a major record of his working life
Six numbered symphonies and Manfred; three ballets; operas, concertos, chamber music, piano music and songs
composer.background:
Tchaikovsky was born at Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. Music belonged to the household before it became a profession: his governess Fanny Dürbach remembered the child’s intense responses to it, and he began piano lessons early. His formal training nevertheless pointed towards government service. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg, separated from his family. His mother died of cholera in 1854. After graduating in 1859 he worked in the Ministry of Justice, while concerts, opera and lessons gradually occupied more of his time.

When Anton Rubinstein’s Saint Petersburg Conservatory opened in 1862, Tchaikovsky joined its first generation of students. He studied composition with Rubinstein and theoretical subjects with Nikolai Zaremba, leaving government employment in 1863. The training mattered practically: he could organise large forms, prepare orchestral scores and teach harmony. In 1866 Nikolai Rubinstein recruited him for the new Moscow Conservatory. Tchaikovsky taught there until 1878, wrote criticism and translated pedagogical material. His early reputation grew through this sustained professional work.
